docs.title: RdfColumn
docs.text:
Column of RDF terms: the cells of one statement position (Jelly-RDF) or one variable (Jelly-SPARQL) across all rows of a batch, in row order. A cell is either an RDF term or unbound.

Each run of consecutive equal terms is stored once, as a run value, and unbound cells are not stored. The run values are split by type into separate lists. kinds gives the type of each run value, and layouts gives the runs of repeated values and of unbound cells.

Used by the column layout and by Jelly-SPARQL.

Field Type Label Description kinds bytes Type of each run value, 2 bits per value, four values per byte, starting from the least significant bits: 0 = IRI, 1 = literal, 2 = blank node, 3 = triple term. Should be empty if all run values are of one type. layouts uint32 repeated Sequence layout: where the run values repeat, and where the unbound cells are. Each entry is a token (skip << 5) name_ids uint32 repeated Name identifiers of the IRIs, in row order. 0 means "previous name_id + 1", or 1 in the first IRI of the column. prefix_ids uint32 repeated Prefix identifiers of the IRIs: none (no prefix), one (the same prefix for all IRIs), or one per IRI. 0 means "the same prefix as the previous IRI", or no prefix in the first IRI of the column. lex_values string repeated Lexical forms of the literals, in row order. literal_kinds uint32 repeated Literal kinds of the literals: none (all are simple literals), one (the same kind for all literals), or one per literal. 0 – simple literal (xsd:string) odd v – literal with the datatype (v + 1) / 2 of the datatype lookup even v > 0 – language-tagged string with the language tag langtags[v / 2 - 1] langtags string repeated Language tags referred to by literal_kinds. langtag_directions uint32 repeated Base directions of the language tags (RdfBaseDirection values), parallel to langtags. Empty means no base direction for any tag. bnodes string repeated Labels of the blank nodes, in row order. triple_terms RdfTripleTerm repeated Triple terms, in row order. The IRIs inside the triple terms are inferred separately from name_ids and prefix_ids.

docs.title: RdfColumnBatch
docs.text:
The contents of a frame in the column layout: a batch of statements, and the lookup entries and namespace declarations they need.

Each statement is made up of the cells at the same position in the subjects, predicates, objects, and graphs columns.

Field Type Label Description row_count uint32 Number of statements in the batch. At most 2^27 - 1. names RdfLookupEntryPacked repeated Entries of the name lookup table. prefixes RdfLookupEntryPacked repeated Entries of the prefix lookup table. Note: the prefixes in the lookup table can be arbitrary strings, and are NOT meant to be user-facing. They are only used for IRI compression. To transmit user-facing namespace declarations, use namespaces. datatypes RdfLookupEntryPacked repeated Entries of the datatype lookup table. namespaces RdfNamespaceDeclaration repeated Namespace declarations. subjects RdfColumn Subjects: IRIs or blank nodes. No cell may be unbound. predicates RdfColumn Predicates: IRIs. No cell may be unbound. objects RdfColumn Objects: IRIs, blank nodes, literals, or triple terms. No cell may be unbound. graphs RdfColumn Graph names: IRIs or blank nodes. An unbound cell is the default graph. Only valid if the physical type is QUADS. If not set, all statements of the batch are in the default graph. message_lengths uint32 repeated Message boundaries: each value adds that many more statements to the current RDF Message, and then ends it. Only valid in streams of type RDF_STREAM_TYPE_MESSAGES.

docs.title: RdfDatatypeEntry
docs.text:
Entry in the datatype lookup table

Not used in the column layout.

Field Type Label Description id uint32 1-based identifier If id=0, it should be interpreted as previous_id + 1. If id=0 appears in the first RdfDatatypeEntry of the stream, it should be interpreted as 1. value string Value of the datatype (UTF-8 encoded)

docs.title: RdfDefaultGraph
docs.text:
Empty message indicating the default RDF graph.

Not used in the column layout.

docs.title: RdfGraphEnd
docs.text:
End of a graph in a GRAPHS stream

Not used in the column layout.

docs.title: RdfGraphStart
docs.text:
Start of a graph in a GRAPHS stream

In contrast to RdfQuad, setting the graph oneof to some value is always required. No repeated terms are allowed.

Not used in the column layout.

Field Type Label Description g_iri RdfIri IRI g_bnode string Blank node g_default_graph RdfDefaultGraph Default graph g_literal RdfLiteral Literal – only valid for generalized RDF streams

docs.title: RdfIri
docs.text:
RDF IRI, encoded as a prefix and a name from the lookup tables. The IRI is the prefix followed by the name.

Field Type Label Description prefix_id uint32 1-based identifier of the prefix in the prefix lookup. 0 means "the same prefix as in the previous IRI", or no prefix in the first IRI. Which IRI is the previous one depends on the layout. name_id uint32 1-based identifier of the name in the name lookup. 0 means "the name_id of the previous IRI + 1", or 1 in the first IRI.

docs.title: RdfLiteral
docs.text:
RDF literal

Field Type Label Description lex string The lexical form of the literal. langtag string Language tag of a language-tagged string. datatype uint32 1-based identifier of the datatype in the datatype lookup. 0 is invalid (in contrast to prefix_id and name_id in RdfIri). If column layout: must not refer to rdf:langString or rdf:dirLangString. direction RdfBaseDirection Base direction of a language-tagged string (RDF 1.2). If column layout: may be set only if langtag is set. If row layout: must not be set.

docs.title: RdfLookupEntryPacked
docs.text:
Packed entries of a lookup table (name, prefix, or datatype): the values of a run of consecutive identifiers.

Used by the column layout and by Jelly-SPARQL.

Field Type Label Description id uint32 1-based identifier of the first value. 0 means "the identifier after the last value of the previous entry of the same lookup table", or 1 in the first entry of the table. values string repeated Values of the entries (UTF-8 encoded), for consecutive identifiers starting at id.

docs.title: RdfNameEntry
docs.text:
Entry in the name lookup table

Not used in the column layout.

Field Type Label Description id uint32 1-based identifier If id=0, it should be interpreted as previous_id + 1. If id=0 appears in the first RdfNameEntry of the stream, it should be interpreted as 1. value string Value of the name (UTF-8 encoded)

docs.title: RdfNamespaceDeclaration
docs.text:
Explicit namespace declaration

This is a hint to the consumer that the given IRI (namespace) may be associated with a short name, like in Turtle syntax: PREFIX ex: <http://example.org/>

This is a purely cosmetic feature, not part of the RDF data. It has nothing in common with the prefix lookup table. A declaration stays in effect until the same name is declared again.

Field Type Label Description name string Short name of the namespace (e.g., "ex") Do NOT include the colon. value RdfIri IRI of the namespace (e.g., "http://example.org/"))

docs.title: RdfPrefixEntry
docs.text:
Entry in the prefix lookup table

Note: the prefixes in the lookup table can be arbitrary strings, and are NOT meant to be user-facing. They are only used for IRI compression. To transmit user-facing namespace declarations for cosmetic purposes, use RdfNamespaceDeclaration.

Not used in the column layout.

Field Type Label Description id uint32 1-based identifier If id=0, it should be interpreted as previous_id + 1. If id=0 appears in the first RdfPrefixEntry of the stream, it should be interpreted as 1. value string Value of the prefix (UTF-8 encoded)

docs.title: RdfQuad
docs.text:
RDF quad

Fields 1–12 are repeated from RdfTriple for performance reasons.

Similarly to RdfTriple, this message allows for representing generalized RDF quads (for example, with literals as predicates). Whether this is used in the stream is determined by the stream options (see RdfStreamOptions).

If no field in a given oneof is set, the term is interpreted as a repeated term – the same as the term in the same position in the previous quad. In the first quad of the stream, all terms must be set.

Not used in the column layout.

Field Type Label Description s_iri RdfIri IRI s_bnode string Blank node s_literal RdfLiteral Literal Only valid in a generalized RDF stream. s_triple_term RdfTriple RDF-star quoted triple p_iri RdfIri IRI p_bnode string Blank node Only valid in a generalized RDF stream. p_literal RdfLiteral Literal Only valid in a generalized RDF stream. p_triple_term RdfTriple RDF-star quoted triple o_iri RdfIri IRI o_bnode string Blank node o_literal RdfLiteral Literal o_triple_term RdfTriple RDF-star quoted triple g_iri RdfIri IRI g_bnode string Blank node g_default_graph RdfDefaultGraph Default graph g_literal RdfLiteral Literal – only valid for generalized RDF streams

docs.title: RdfStreamFrame
docs.text:
RDF stream frame – base message for RDF streams.

Field Type Label Description rows RdfStreamRow repeated Stream rows. If row layout: the contents of the frame. If column layout: either empty, or exactly one row with the stream options. columns RdfColumnBatch If column layout: the contents of the frame. If row layout: must not be set. metadata RdfStreamFrame.MetadataEntry repeated Arbitrary metadata The keys are UTF-8 encoded strings, the values are byte arrays. This may be used by implementations in any way they see fit. The metadata does not affect the RDF data in any way, treat it as comments in a text file.

docs.title: RdfStreamFrame.MetadataEntry
docs.text: Field Type Label Description key string value bytes

docs.title: RdfStreamOptions
docs.text:
RDF stream options

If row layout: the options may occur again later in the stream, but must be identical to the first occurrence. If column layout: a later frame may restate the options, which empties the lookup tables. This makes streams concatenable. physical_type, stream_type, and version must stay the same.

Field Type Label Description stream_name string Name of the stream (completely optional). This may be used for, e.g., topic names in a pub/sub system. physical_type PhysicalStreamType Type of the stream (required). If row layout: TRIPLES, QUADS, or GRAPHS. If column layout: TRIPLES or QUADS. generalized_statements bool If row layout: whether the stream may contain generalized triples, quads, or datasets. If column layout: must not be set. rdf_star bool If row layout: whether the stream may contain RDF-star statements. If column layout: must not be set – use rdf_version instead. stream_type RdfStreamType If column layout: whether the stream is one RDF graph or dataset, or a stream of RDF Messages. Defaults to RDF_STREAM_TYPE_FLAT. If row layout: must not be set. rdf_version RdfVersion If column layout: version of RDF whose terms may occur in the stream. Unspecified (the default) means that no version is announced, and the stream may contain any RDF 1.2 term. If row layout: must not be set. max_name_table_size uint32 Maximum size of the name lookup table (required). If row layout: must be >= 8. If column layout: must be >= 128. max_prefix_table_size uint32 Maximum size of the prefix lookup table (required if the prefix lookup is used) max_datatype_table_size uint32 Maximum size of the datatype lookup table (required if datatype literals are used) logical_type LogicalStreamType If row layout: logical (RDF-STaX-based) stream type. In contrast to the physical type, this field is entirely optional. If column layout: must not be set – use stream_type instead. version uint32 Protocol version (required) For Jelly-RDF 1.0.x the value must be 1 (row layout). For Jelly-RDF 1.1.x the value must be 2 (row layout). For Jelly-RDF 1.2.x the value must be 3 (column layout). For custom extensions, the value must be 10000 or higher.

docs.title: RdfStreamRow
docs.text:
RDF stream row

If row layout: one element of a frame. If column layout: only the options field may be set.

Field Type Label Description options RdfStreamOptions Stream options. Must occur at the start of the stream. triple RdfTriple RDF triple statement. Valid in streams of physical type TRIPLES or GRAPHS. quad RdfQuad RDF quad statement. Only valid in streams of physical type QUADS. graph_start RdfGraphStart Graph boundary: ends the currently transmitted graph and starts a new one Only valid in streams of physical type GRAPHS. graph_end RdfGraphEnd Explicit end of a graph. Signals the consumer that the transmitted graph is complete. Only valid in streams of physical type GRAPHS. namespace RdfNamespaceDeclaration Explicit namespace declaration. name RdfNameEntry Entry in the name lookup table. prefix RdfPrefixEntry Entry in the prefix lookup table. datatype RdfDatatypeEntry Entry in the datatype lookup table.

docs.title: RdfTriple
docs.text:
RDF triple

For each term (subject, predicate, object), the fields are repeated for performance reasons. This is to avoid the need for boxing each term in a separate message.

Note: this message allows for representing generalized RDF triples (for example, with literals as predicates). Whether this is used in the stream is determined by the stream options (see RdfStreamOptions).

If no field in a given oneof is set, the term is interpreted as a repeated term – the same as the term in the same position in the previous triple. In the first triple of the stream, all terms must be set. All terms must also be set in quoted triples (RDF-star).

Not used in the column layout.

Field Type Label Description s_iri RdfIri IRI s_bnode string Blank node s_literal RdfLiteral Literal Only valid in a generalized RDF stream. s_triple_term RdfTriple RDF-star quoted triple p_iri RdfIri IRI p_bnode string Blank node Only valid in a generalized RDF stream. p_literal RdfLiteral Literal Only valid in a generalized RDF stream. p_triple_term RdfTriple RDF-star quoted triple o_iri RdfIri IRI o_bnode string Blank node o_literal RdfLiteral Literal o_triple_term RdfTriple RDF-star quoted triple

docs.title: RdfTripleTerm
docs.text:
RDF 1.2 triple term. All three positions must be set, and only the object may be a nested triple term. The field numbers are the same as in RdfTriple.

Used by the column layout and by Jelly-SPARQL.

Field Type Label Description s_iri RdfIri IRI s_bnode string Blank node p_iri RdfIri Predicate o_iri RdfIri IRI o_bnode string Blank node o_literal RdfLiteral Literal o_triple_term RdfTripleTerm Nested triple term

docs.title: LogicalStreamType
docs.text:
Logical stream type, according to the RDF Stream Taxonomy (RDF-STaX). If column layout: not used – use RdfStreamType instead.

Type 0 is reserved for the unspecified stream type. The rest of the type numbers follow the taxonomical structure of RDF-STaX. For example: 1 is a subtype of 0, 13 and 23 are subtypes of 3, 114 is a subtype of 14, etc.

Types 1–4 correspond to the four base concrete stream types. Their subtypes can be in most cases simply processed in the same way as the base types. Therefore, implementations can take the modulo 10 of the stream type to determine the base type of the stream and use this information to select the appropriate processing logic.

RDF-STaX version: 1.1.2 https://w3id.org/stax/1.1.2

Not used in the column layout.

Name Number Description LOGICAL_STREAM_TYPE_UNSPECIFIED 0 Unspecified stream type – invalid LOGICAL_STREAM_TYPE_FLAT_TRIPLES 1 Flat RDF triple stream https://w3id.org/stax/ontology#flatTripleStream LOGICAL_STREAM_TYPE_FLAT_QUADS 2 Flat RDF quad stream https://w3id.org/stax/ontology#flatQuadStream LOGICAL_STREAM_TYPE_GRAPHS 3 RDF graph stream https://w3id.org/stax/ontology#graphStream LOGICAL_STREAM_TYPE_DATASETS 4 RDF dataset stream https://w3id.org/stax/ontology#datasetStream LOGICAL_STREAM_TYPE_SUBJECT_GRAPHS 13 RDF subject graph stream (subtype of RDF graph stream) https://w3id.org/stax/ontology#subjectGraphStream LOGICAL_STREAM_TYPE_NAMED_GRAPHS 14 RDF named graph stream (subtype of RDF dataset stream) https://w3id.org/stax/ontology#namedGraphStream LOGICAL_STREAM_TYPE_TIMESTAMPED_NAMED_GRAPHS 114 RDF timestamped named graph stream (subtype of RDF dataset stream) https://w3id.org/stax/ontology#timestampedNamedGraphStream

docs.title: PhysicalStreamType
docs.text:
Physical stream type: whether the stream contains triples or quads.

Name Number Description PHYSICAL_STREAM_TYPE_UNSPECIFIED 0 Unspecified stream type – invalid PHYSICAL_STREAM_TYPE_TRIPLES 1 RDF triples PHYSICAL_STREAM_TYPE_QUADS 2 RDF quads PHYSICAL_STREAM_TYPE_GRAPHS 3 RDF triples grouped in graphs. If column layout: invalid.

docs.title: RdfBaseDirection
docs.text:
Initial text direction of a language-tagged string (RDF 1.2).

Name Number Description RDF_BASE_DIRECTION_UNSPECIFIED 0 No base direction: an ordinary language-tagged string (rdf:langString). RDF_BASE_DIRECTION_LTR 1 Left-to-right ("ltr"): a directional language-tagged string (rdf:dirLangString). RDF_BASE_DIRECTION_RTL 2 Right-to-left ("rtl"): a directional language-tagged string (rdf:dirLangString).

docs.title: RdfStreamType
docs.text:
Type of an RDF stream. Not used in the row layout.

Name Number Description RDF_STREAM_TYPE_FLAT 0 The entire stream is one RDF graph (TRIPLES) or one RDF dataset (QUADS). This is the default. buf:lint:ignore ENUM_ZERO_VALUE_SUFFIX RDF_STREAM_TYPE_MESSAGES 1 The stream is a sequence of RDF Messages, each an RDF graph or dataset: https://w3c-cg.github.io/rsp/spec/messages The messages are delimited by RdfColumnBatch.message_lengths.

docs.title: RdfVersion
docs.text:
Version of RDF that a stream conforms to, following the version labels of RDF 1.2 Concepts: https://www.w3.org/TR/rdf12-concepts/#defined-version-labels

Name Number Description RDF_VERSION_UNSPECIFIED 0 Unspecified. Each format that uses this enum defines how to interpret it. RDF_VERSION_1_1 1 RDF 1.1 (version label "1.1"): no triple terms, no base directions. RDF_VERSION_1_2_BASIC 2 RDF 1.2 Basic (version label "1.2-basic"): base directions are allowed, triple terms are not. RDF_VERSION_1_2 3 RDF 1.2 (version label "1.2"): base directions and triple terms are allowed.

Top

docs.title: SparqlAskResult
docs.text:
Boolean result of a SPARQL ASK query.

Field Type Label Description value bool The boolean value of the result.

docs.title: SparqlResultsFrame
docs.text:
SPARQL results frame – base message of a SPARQL result stream. A frame contains a batch of rows (solutions).

Field Type Label Description options SparqlResultsOptions Stream options. Must be set in the first frame of the stream. May be set again in a later frame, which empties the lookup tables. variables string repeated Result set header: the names of the variables, in projection (SELECT clause) order, without the leading "?" or "$". Set in the first frame of a result set with a solution sequence, and in a frame that contains the options. row_count uint32 Number of rows (solutions) in this frame. At most 2^27 - 1. names eu.ostrzyciel.jelly.core.proto.v1.RdfLookupEntryPacked repeated Entries in the name lookup table. prefixes eu.ostrzyciel.jelly.core.proto.v1.RdfLookupEntryPacked repeated Entries in the prefix lookup table. Note: the prefixes in the lookup table can be arbitrary strings, and are NOT meant to be user-facing. They are only used for IRI compression. datatypes eu.ostrzyciel.jelly.core.proto.v1.RdfLookupEntryPacked repeated Entries in the datatype lookup table. columns eu.ostrzyciel.jelly.core.proto.v1.RdfColumn repeated Columns, one per variable, in the order of variables, or none. ask_result SparqlAskResult Boolean (ASK) result. If set, the result set is a boolean result instead of a solution sequence. A boolean result is always the only frame of its result set. trailer SparqlResultsTrailer End-of-result-set marker. See SparqlResultsTrailer. metadata SparqlResultsFrame.MetadataEntry repeated Arbitrary metadata The keys are UTF-8 encoded strings, the values are byte arrays. The metadata does not affect the result data in any way, treat it as comments in a text file. Well-known keys (their values must be valid UTF-8): link – zero or more IRIs separated by LF (U+000A), describing the result set as a whole (not the frame). Corresponds to head.link in the SPARQL Query Results JSON format. All other keys may be used by implementations in any way they see fit, and their values are arbitrary bytes.

docs.title: SparqlResultsFrame.MetadataEntry
docs.text: Field Type Label Description key string value bytes

docs.title: SparqlResultsOptions
docs.text:
Stream options for SPARQL result streams.

Field Type Label Description stream_name string Name of the stream (completely optional). This may be used for, e.g., topic names in a pub/sub system. stream_type SparqlStreamType Type of the stream: one result set, or a sequence of result sets. Defaults to SPARQL_STREAM_TYPE_FLAT. rdf_version eu.ostrzyciel.jelly.core.proto.v1.RdfVersion Version of RDF whose terms may occur in the stream. RDF_VERSION_1_1 – no triple terms, no base directions RDF_VERSION_1_2_BASIC – base directions, no triple terms RDF_VERSION_1_2 – base directions and triple terms Unspecified (the default) means that no version is announced: the stream may contain any RDF 1.2 term. max_name_table_size uint32 Maximum size of the name lookup table (required, must be >= 128) max_prefix_table_size uint32 Maximum size of the prefix lookup table (required if the prefix lookup is used) max_datatype_table_size uint32 Maximum size of the datatype lookup table (required if datatype literals are used) version uint32 Protocol version (required) For Jelly-SPARQL 1.0.x, the value must be 1. For custom extensions, the value must be 10000 or higher.

docs.title: SparqlResultsTrailer
docs.text:
End-of-result-set marker, saying whether the result set is complete. Producers must write it in the last frame of every result set, unless they cannot write anything more at all (for example, because the process died).

Field Type Label Description error string Empty (the default) means the result set is complete. A non-empty value is a human-readable explanation of why the producer could not complete the result set (e.g., query failure mid-evaluation).

docs.title: SparqlStreamType
docs.text:
Type of a SPARQL result stream.

Name Number Description SPARQL_STREAM_TYPE_FLAT 0 The entire stream is a single result set. This is the default. buf:lint:ignore ENUM_ZERO_VALUE_SUFFIX SPARQL_STREAM_TYPE_PUNCTUATED 1 The stream is a sequence of result sets, each ended by a frame with a trailer. The lookup tables are kept from one result set to the next.

docs.title: Jelly RDF serialization format specification
docs.text:
This document is the specification of the Jelly RDF serialization format, also known as Jelly-RDF, version 1.2. It is intended for implementers of Jelly libraries and applications. If you are looking for a user-friendly introduction to Jelly, see the Jelly index page.

This document is accompanied by the Jelly Protobuf reference and the Protobuf definition itself (rdf.proto).

Jelly-RDF 1.0 and 1.1

This document describes only Jelly-RDF 1.2. Jelly-RDF 1.0.x and 1.1.x store the stream frames differently (in the row layout), as described in the Jelly-RDF 1.1 specification. See the Earlier versions section for more details.

The following assumptions are used in this document:

  • The basis for the terms used is the RDF 1.2 Concepts and Abstract Data Model specification (W3C Candidate Recommendation Snapshot 07 April 2026). The format also supports RDF 1.1 – see RDF version.
  • Additionally, the RDF 1.2 Turtle specification (W3C Working Draft 07 October 2026) is used in parts as a basis for selected definitions.
  • In parts referring to RDF Messages, the latest version of the RDF Messages specification is used.
  • All strings in the serialization are assumed to be UTF-8 encoded.
Document information Authors: Piotr Sowiński (Ostrzyciel), Anastasiya Danilenka (adanilenka) Version: dev Date: October 19, 2026 Permanent URL: https://w3id.org/jelly/dev/specification/serialization Document status: Draft specification (use the version selector on the top bar to find a stable specification) License: CC BY 4.0

Info

The key words "MUST", "MUST NOT", "REQUIRED", "SHOULD", "SHOULD NOT", "RECOMMENDED", "MAY", and "OPTIONAL" in this document are to be interpreted as described in RFC 2119.

Note

The "Note" blocks in this document are not part of the specification, but rather provide additional information for implementers.

Note

The "Example" blocks in this document are not part of the specification, but rather provide informal examples of the serialization format.

docs.title: Conformance
docs.text:
Implementations MAY choose to implement only a subset of the following specification. In this case, they SHOULD clearly specify which parts of the specification they implement. In the rest of this specification, the keywords "MUST", "MUST NOT", etc. refer to full (not partial) implementations.

Note

Implementations may in particular choose to not implement features that are not supported on the target platform (e.g., RDF datasets, RDF-star, generalized RDF terms, etc.).

Implementations MAY also choose to extend Jelly with additional features that SHOULD NOT interfere with the serialization being readable by implementations which follow the specification.

To claim conformance with this specification, an implementation MUST pass all applicable tests from the Jelly-RDF conformance test suite (and, for reading Jelly-RDF 1.0 and 1.1 streams, from the Jelly-RDF 1.1 test suite), and MUST provide a conformance report as described on the reporting conformance page. Implementations SHOULD pass the conformance tests marked with the SHOULD conformance level (jellyt:featureShouldLevel).

Note

Conformance tests are a way to verify that implementations correctly follow the specification. However, passing all tests does not guarantee that the implementation perfectly implements the specification, is free of bugs, or that it will work in all scenarios.

Implementations typically also employ extensive unit tests, integration tests, and other quality assurance measures to ensure correctness and reliability.

docs.title: Versioning
docs.text:
The protocol follows the Semantic Versioning 2.0 scheme. Each MAJOR.MINOR semantic version corresponds to an integer version tag in the protocol. The version tag is encoded in the version field of the RdfStreamOptions message. See also the section on the version tag for more information on how to handle the version tags in serialized streams.

The following versions of the protocol are defined:

Version tag Semantic version Release date Changes 1 1.0.x August 24, 2024 (initial version) 2 1.1.0 December 21, 2024 Added RdfNamespaceDeclaration 2 1.1.1 March 10, 2025 Added RdfStreamFrame.metadata 2 1.1.2 June 12, 2025 Bugfixes: #35, #43, #44 2 1.1.3 September 30, 2025 Added the conformance test suite 3 1.2.0 (current) October 19, 2026 (in development) New column layout of stream frames, RDF 1.2, RDF Messages, concatenable streams. See changes from Jelly-RDF 1.1.

Note

Releases of the protocol are published on GitHub.

docs.title: Earlier versions
docs.text:
Streams with version tag 1 or 2 (Jelly-RDF 1.0.x and 1.1.x) use the row layout, in which a stream frame is a list of rows, containing statements and lookup entries. Streams with version tag 3 (Jelly-RDF 1.2.x) use the column layout described in this document. Both layouts use the same Protobuf messages for stream frames and stream options, so a consumer can determine which layout is in use by examining the version field of the stream options.

  • If the stream options of a stream have version tag 1 or 2, the consumer MUST read the stream as described in the Jelly-RDF 1.1 specification. This document does not apply to such a stream.
  • A producer MAY write a stream with version tag 1 or 2, for example so that consumers that support only Jelly-RDF 1.0 or 1.1 can read it. It MUST then follow the Jelly-RDF 1.1 specification, and this document does not apply to that stream.
  • In a stream with version tag 1 or 2, the fields added in Jelly-RDF 1.2 MUST NOT be set: RdfStreamFrame.columns, RdfStreamOptions.stream_type, RdfStreamOptions.rdf_version, and RdfLiteral.direction. The consumer MAY ignore these fields if they are set.

Following the backward compatibility rules, a consumer that fully implements this specification MUST be able to read streams with version tags 1 and 2.

docs.title: Backward compatibility
docs.text:
Implementations SHOULD ensure backward compatibility. To achieve backward compatibility, the implementation MUST be able to read all messages from the previous releases of the protocol with the same MAJOR version. The implementation MAY also be able to read messages from previous releases of the protocol with a different MAJOR version.

Note

The protocol is designed in such a way that you don't need to worry about backward compatibility. The only thing you need to do is to implement the latest version of the protocol, and you will automatically get backward compatibility with all previous versions (of the same MAJOR).

docs.title: Forward compatibility
docs.text:
Forward compatibility is not guaranteed across different MINOR versions of the protocol. Implementations MAY be able to read messages from future releases of the protocol with the same MAJOR version. Implementations MAY also be able to read messages from future releases of the protocol with a different MAJOR version.

New features introduced in PATCH versions of the protocol MUST NOT break forward compatibility.

Note

In practical terms, new MINOR versions of the protocol introduce features that previous implementations do not know how to handle. Implementations will generally refuse to read a stream that is marked as using a higher protocol version than they support (see: version tag).

Forward-compatible features

Protobuf allows for adding new fields to messages without breaking compatibility with older implementations – they will simply ignore the new field. An example of this is the metadata field in the RdfStreamFrame message, which was added in version 1.1.1. Implementations of version 1.1.0 ignore it.

docs.title: Actors and implementations
docs.text:
Jelly-RDF assumes there to be two actors involved in processing the stream: the producer (serializer) and the consumer (parser). The producer is responsible for serializing the RDF data into the Jelly format, and the consumer is responsible for parsing the Jelly format into RDF data.

Implementations may include only the producer, only the consumer, or both.

docs.title: Format specification
docs.text:
The Jelly RDF serialization format uses Protocol Buffers version 3 as the underlying serialization format. All implementations MUST use a compliant Protocol Buffers implementation. The Protocol Buffers schema for Jelly serialization is defined in rdf.proto (source code, reference).

The Jelly-RDF format describes a stream (i.e., an ordered sequence) of stream frames. The frames may be sent one-by-one using a dedicated streaming protocol (e.g., gRPC, MQTT, Kafka) or written in sequence to a byte stream (e.g., a file or socket). When writing multiple frames to a byte stream, the frames MUST be delimited – see the delimited variant.

A stream contains RDF statements: triples or quads, depending on the physical stream type. The whole stream is either one RDF graph or dataset, or a sequence of RDF Messages, depending on the stream type.

Within a frame, the RDF terms of statements are stored in columns: all subjects of the frame in one column, then all predicates, all objects, and all graph names. Within a column, the values of each type of RDF term are stored in their own flat lists. IRIs and datatypes are compressed using lookup tables.

Why columns?

In a row-oriented layout, every term needs its own length-delimited sub-message with a oneof selecting the term type, which costs additional bytes on the wire and memory on the consumer's side. Grouping the values of one position in a column lets us amortize this cost. If all values in a column are of the same type, there is no additional cost, and 2 bits per value otherwise (see term types). Values that repeat in consecutive statements (e.g., the same subject or graph) can be compressed efficiently (see sequence layout), and a consumer can keep the values of a column in primitive arrays.

Messages used only by Jelly-RDF 1.0 and 1.1

rdf.proto also contains messages used only by the row layout of Jelly-RDF 1.0.x and 1.1.x (and by Jelly-Patch): RdfTriple, RdfQuad, RdfGraphStart, RdfGraphEnd, RdfDefaultGraph, RdfNameEntry, RdfPrefixEntry, RdfDatatypeEntry, LogicalStreamType, and all fields of RdfStreamRow except options. They are not used in Jelly-RDF 1.2 streams and are not described in this document.

docs.title: Stream types
docs.text:
The stream type indicates whether the stream is one RDF graph or dataset, or a sequence of RDF Messages. It is set in the stream_type field (5) of the stream options, as an RdfStreamType value:

  • RDF_STREAM_TYPE_FLAT (0) – default value. The entire stream is one RDF graph (physical type TRIPLES) or one RDF dataset (physical type QUADS). Blank node labels are scoped to the whole stream. Message boundaries MUST NOT be used. The consumer SHOULD throw an error otherwise.
  • RDF_STREAM_TYPE_MESSAGES (1) – the stream is an RDF Message Stream or RDF Message Log. Each message is an RDF graph (physical type TRIPLES) or an RDF dataset (physical type QUADS). The messages are delimited by message boundaries. Blank node labels are scoped to one message. The lookup tables and the namespace declarations are kept from one message to the next.

An RDF Message is a unit of RDF data, as defined by the RDF Messages specification. One RDF Message may span many stream frames, and one frame may contain many RDF Messages.

Support for the RDF_STREAM_TYPE_MESSAGES stream type is OPTIONAL. A consumer that does not support it SHOULD throw an error when it reads stream options with this stream type.

Consumers MUST throw an error if the stream type has a value that is not listed above.

docs.title: Stream frames
docs.text:
A stream frame is a message of type RdfStreamFrame (reference). It has the following fields:

  • rows (1) – either empty, or exactly one RdfStreamRow message with the options field set, containing the stream options. The consumer SHOULD throw an error if rows contains more than one row, or a row with a field other than options set.
  • columns (2) – the contents of the frame, as an RdfColumnBatch message – see column batches. This field is OPTIONAL. A frame without it contains no statements.
  • metadata (15) – stream frame metadata.

If the frame has the stream options, they MUST be processed before the column batch of the same frame.

A frame that has no rows and no column batch is an empty frame. Empty frames are valid, and have no effect on the RDF data.

A stream frame may contain any number of statements, however it is RECOMMENDED to keep the serialized size of the frames below 1 MB.

The frames have no meaning of their own – they are purely a batching mechanism. In particular, in a stream of RDF Messages, the frame boundaries are not message boundaries: the messages are delimited explicitly (see message boundaries).

Note

Because a frame is just a batch of statements, the producer is free to choose the batch size. The producer may also have to end a frame early, when the lookup tables fill up.

docs.title: Ordering
docs.text:
Stream frames MUST be processed strictly in order to preserve the semantics of the stream. Each stream frame MUST be processed in its entirety before the next stream frame is processed.

Implementations MAY choose to adopt a non-standard solution where the order or delivery of the frames is not guaranteed and the stream can be read in more than one order or without some frames. The implementation MUST clearly specify in the documentation that it uses such a non-standard solution.

Note

An example where not adhering to the strict ordering may be useful is when you are dealing with a network streaming protocol that does not guarantee the order of the messages (e.g., MQTT).

Making frames independently decodable

The main thing you will need to worry about is the state of the lookup tables. If you can, emit all lookup entries at the beginning of the stream. When using stream partitions (e.g., in Kafka), you should ensure that the lookup entries are emitted to each partition. Alternatively, you can transmit the lookup entries separately from the stream.

Because the IRI inference state resets per column, per batch, a frame can be decoded using only the stream options and the state of the lookup tables. A producer that re-emits all the lookup entries it needs in every frame makes each frame decodable on its own, given the stream options. This costs space, allows for building a stream whose frames can be dropped or processed out of order.

docs.title: Stream frame metadata
docs.text:
RdfStreamFrame messages have a metadata field (15) of type map<string, bytes>. This field is OPTIONAL and does not influence the processing of RDF data in any manner. The keys and values in the map are arbitrary and implementation-defined.

Consumers SHOULD ignore unknown keys in the metadata map. Consumers also SHOULD validate the values in the metadata map to ensure that they follow the expected format. Consumers MUST NOT assume that values are character strings or that they are valid UTF-8.

Note

The metadata field is intended for use cases where additional information about the stream frame must be attached directly to the stream, but not as part of the RDF stream itself. For example, you could use it to store the timestamp of the frame, its unique identifier, hash code, or anything else relevant to your use case.

You can use the metadata to store UTF-8 strings, numbers, or even nested protobuf messages. Because of this, you should never assume that the value is a valid string. Always validate the value before using it.

docs.title: Stream options
docs.text:
The stream options is a message of type RdfStreamOptions (reference), stored in the rows field of a stream frame. It communicates to the consumer the type of the stream, RDF features used in it, sizes of the lookup tables needed to decode it, and the version of the protocol.

The producer MUST put the stream options in the first non-empty frame of the stream, that is, the first frame that has rows or a column batch. A later frame MAY restate the stream options.

The consumer MAY throw an error if a column batch is encountered before any stream options. Alternatively, it MAY use its own, implementation-specified default options.

The stream options message contains the following fields:

  • stream_name (1) – name of the stream. This field is OPTIONAL and the manner in which it should be used is not defined by this specification. It MAY be used to identify the stream.
  • physical_type (2) – physical type of the stream. This field is REQUIRED.
  • generalized_statements (3), rdf_star (4), and logical_type (14) – these fields are used only in Jelly-RDF 1.0.x and 1.1.x. They MUST NOT be set (i.e., they must have their default values). The consumer SHOULD throw an error if any of them is set.
  • stream_type (5) – the stream type. This field is OPTIONAL and defaults to RDF_STREAM_TYPE_FLAT.
  • rdf_version (6) – the version of RDF whose terms may occur in the stream. This field is OPTIONAL and defaults to RDF_VERSION_UNSPECIFIED.
  • max_name_table_size (9) – maximum size of the name lookup. This field is REQUIRED and MUST be set to a value greater than or equal to 128. The consumer SHOULD throw an error otherwise. The size of the name lookup MUST NOT exceed the value of this field.
  • max_prefix_table_size (10) – maximum size of the prefix lookup. This field is OPTIONAL and defaults to 0 (no lookup). If the field is set to 0, the prefix lookup MUST NOT be used in the stream, and the consumer SHOULD throw an error if it is. If the field is set to a positive value, the prefix lookup SHOULD be used in the stream and the size of the prefix lookup MUST NOT exceed the value of this field.
  • max_datatype_table_size (11) – maximum size of the datatype lookup. This field is OPTIONAL and defaults to 0 (no lookup). If the field is set to 0, the datatype lookup MUST NOT be used in the stream, which effectively prohibits the use of datatype literals. The consumer SHOULD throw an error if it is used. If the field is set to a positive value, the datatype lookup SHOULD be used in the stream and the size of the lookup MUST NOT exceed the value of this field.
  • version (15) – version tag of the stream. This field is REQUIRED. For streams that follow this specification, it MUST be set to 3.

This specification sets no upper bound on the lookup table sizes. Instead, each consumer SHOULD define the largest tables it is willing to allocate and reject a stream that asks for more – see security considerations. The RECOMMENDED defaults are 16384 names, 4096 prefixes, and 256 datatypes, and consumers SHOULD let the user raise or lower them.

docs.title: Version tag
docs.text:
The following rules apply to the version field of the stream options:

  • The version tag is encoded as a varint. The version tag MUST be greater than 0.
  • The producer of the stream MUST set the version tag to the version tag of the protocol that was used to serialize the stream.
  • The consumer SHOULD throw an error if the version tag is greater than the version tag of the implementation.
  • The consumer SHOULD throw an error if the version tag is zero.
  • The consumer SHOULD NOT throw an error if the version tag is not zero but lower than the version tag of the implementation.
  • The producer may use version tags greater than 10000 to indicate non-standard versions of the protocol.

Streams with version tags 1 and 2 are read as described in earlier versions.

docs.title: Restating the stream options (stream concatenation)
docs.text:
A frame after the first non-empty frame MAY contain the stream options again. This is called restating the stream options. It makes Jelly-RDF 1.2 and newer streams concatenable: a Jelly-RDF file can be appended to another one with the same physical type and stream type without changes, and the result is a valid stream. The other options of the two files, such as the lookup table sizes or the RDF version, may differ. Jelly-RDF 1.0 and 1.1 files cannot be concatenated with Jelly-RDF 1.2 files.

Restating the stream options has the following effects, which take place before the column batch of the same frame is processed:

  • The name, prefix, and datatype lookups are emptied, and their identifier numbering restarts from 1, as at the start of the stream.
  • In a stream of RDF Messages, the current message ends, as it would at the end of the stream (see message boundaries).

Namespace declarations are not reset – they stay in effect. In a FLAT stream, blank node labels are not reset either – a label refers to the same blank node before and after the restated options, as when concatenating N-Triples files.

The physical_type and stream_type fields MUST have the same values in all stream options of a stream. The consumer SHOULD throw an error otherwise. The other fields may differ from the previous stream options, and apply to the frames that follow, until the stream options are restated again. The restated stream options MUST be valid on their own. The consumer MAY throw an error if it does not support the new options (e.g., because they ask for too large lookup tables).

Note

Restating the stream options is not a way for a consumer to join a stream that is already in progress. If you want frames that can be decoded independently, see the note on independently decodable frames instead.

docs.title: Physical stream types
docs.text:
The physical type of the stream MUST be explicitly specified in the stream options. The following types are defined in the PhysicalStreamType enum (reference):

  • PHYSICAL_STREAM_TYPE_UNSPECIFIED (0) – default value. This physical stream type MUST NOT be used. Consumers MUST throw an error if this value is used.
  • PHYSICAL_STREAM_TYPE_TRIPLES (1) – stream of RDF triples. In this case, the column batches MUST NOT have the graphs column set. The consumer SHOULD throw an error otherwise.
  • PHYSICAL_STREAM_TYPE_QUADS (2) – stream of RDF quads: triples, each in the default graph or in a named graph. See column batches for how the graphs are encoded.
  • PHYSICAL_STREAM_TYPE_GRAPHS (3) – used only in Jelly-RDF 1.0.x and 1.1.x. This physical stream type MUST NOT be used. Consumers MUST throw an error if this value is used.

Consumers MUST throw an error if the physical stream type has a value that is not listed above.

Note

In Jelly-RDF 1.1, the GRAPHS type was used to send triples grouped by graph. In Jelly-RDF 1.2, use QUADS instead.

docs.title: RDF version
docs.text:
The rdf_version field (6) of the stream options announces which RDF terms may occur in the stream. Its values follow the version labels of RDF 1.2:

RdfVersion value Version label Base directions Triple terms RDF_VERSION_UNSPECIFIED (0) none ✅ ✅ RDF_VERSION_1_1 (1) 1.1 ❌ ❌ RDF_VERSION_1_2_BASIC (2) 1.2-basic ✅ ❌ RDF_VERSION_1_2 (3) 1.2 ✅ ✅

The following rules apply, following the behavior of other RDF 1.2 serialization formats:

  • If rdf_version is RDF_VERSION_UNSPECIFIED, no version is announced, and the consumer can assume RDF 1.2: the stream MAY contain any term of RDF 1.2.
  • The consumer SHOULD throw an error if rdf_version has a value that is not listed above.
  • Producers SHOULD declare a version when they know in advance which terms the stream may contain. It is RECOMMENDED to declare the lowest version that allows all of these terms. A producer that cannot know this in advance MAY declare a higher version than needed, or MAY leave rdf_version unspecified.
  • If a version is declared, the stream MUST NOT contain a term that the version does not allow. If it does, the consumer MAY throw an error, or it MAY ignore the declared version and read the term.
  • A consumer that does not support the declared version SHOULD throw an error when it reads the stream options.
  • When the stream options are restated, the new rdf_version applies from that frame on.

docs.title: Prefix, name, and datatype lookup entries
docs.text:
Jelly uses a common mechanism of lookup tables for IRI prefixes, IRI names (postfixes), and datatypes. The lookups are used to compress the IRIs and datatypes in the stream. All lookups share the same base mechanism:

  • The lookup is a map from a positive integer (the identifier) to a valid UTF-8 string.
  • The lookups are indexed from 1.
  • The lookup can be modified at any point in the stream, using lookup entries. A lookup entry sets the value for a given identifier. The modification MUST be applied to everything that follows it in the stream (see also the working set of a batch).
  • The first use of a given identifier MUST be after a value is set for it. If the consumer encounters an identifier that has no value in the lookup, it SHOULD throw an error.
  • The maximum size of the lookup is communicated in the stream options. The producer of the stream MUST NOT exceed the maximum size of the lookup. The consumer SHOULD throw an error if a lookup entry has an identifier greater than the maximum size of the lookup. The consumer MAY implement the lookup as a fixed-size array, or extend it dynamically.
  • The lookups are kept from one frame to the next. They are emptied only when the stream options are restated.
  • The producer may use any strategy to update the lookup.

Note

You are free to use any strategy for updating the lookup in the producer. You can use the LRU strategy, LFU, or something more complex. The quality of the strategy will influence the compression ratio and the performance of the system. In general, evicting entries in sequential blocks produces smaller file sizes, because then the producer can use packed lookup entries and compression in IRI sequences.

You can also have a fixed lookup in the producer and communicate it at the start of the stream. This is possible if you are using a fixed set of prefixes, names, or datatypes and want to conserve computing power (e.g., in IoT devices).

The simplest way to implement the consumer's lookup is to just use an indexed array of fixed size.

docs.title: Packed lookup entries
docs.text:
Lookup entries are stored in three fields of RdfColumnBatch, one for each lookup. Each field contains a repeated RdfLookupEntryPacked message:

  • names (2) – entries of the name lookup.
  • prefixes (3) – entries of the prefix lookup.
  • datatypes (4) – entries of the datatype lookup.

Lookup entries are often assigned consecutive identifiers. A packed entry states the identifier once and then lists the values of a whole run of consecutive entries, which saves space.

The RdfLookupEntryPacked message contains the following fields:

  • id (1) – 1-based identifier of the first value in this entry. The default value of 0 MUST be interpreted as previous_id + 1, where previous_id is the identifier of the last value of the previous entry of the same lookup table in the stream. If 0 appears in the first entry of a given lookup table in the stream, or in the first entry after the stream options were restated, it MUST be interpreted as 1.
  • values (2) – the values of the entries, in UTF-8. The first value is assigned the identifier id, and every following value is assigned the identifier of the previous one plus 1.

A packed entry with zero values MUST NOT be written. Consumers MAY throw an error if they encounter one.

Note

The default value of 0 has a special meaning in lookup entries. You should take advantage of that and use it whenever possible. As the value of 0 is encoded with exactly zero bytes, you can save some space by using it.

docs.title: The working set of a batch
docs.text:
All lookup entries of a column batch are applied, in order, before anything else in the batch is decoded. This allows the columns of a batch to be decoded independently of each other.

As a consequence, every lookup identifier referenced by a batch MUST still contain the intended value after all of the batch's entries have been applied. In other words: the working set of a single batch must fit in the lookup tables. A producer MUST NOT overwrite, within one batch, an identifier that the same batch still refers to.

If a producer cannot satisfy this, it MUST end the frame and start a new one. If a single statement cannot be encoded even in an otherwise empty batch, the producer MUST throw an error – the configured lookup table sizes are too small for this data.

Warning

A consumer cannot detect a violation of this rule. It will silently decode the affected terms to the wrong values. This is a producer-side obligation.

Note

A simple way to implement this on the producer's side is to track which identifiers the current batch has touched (assigned or referenced), and to end the frame before a statement could touch an identifier that is already in that set. If the lookup uses an LRU eviction policy, everything the batch has touched resides at the recent end, so the batch stays safe exactly as long as it has not touched every identifier of the table.

docs.title: Column batches
docs.text:
The contents of a stream frame are stored in its columns field, as an RdfColumnBatch message. A column batch contains the following fields:

Field Contents Described in row_count (1) number of statements in the batch this section names (2) entries of the name lookup Packed lookup entries prefixes (3) entries of the prefix lookup Packed lookup entries datatypes (4) entries of the datatype lookup Packed lookup entries namespaces (5) namespace declarations Namespace declarations subjects (6) column of subjects this section, Columns predicates (7) column of predicates this section, Columns objects (8) column of objects this section, Columns graphs (9) column of graph names this section, Columns message_lengths (15) message boundaries Message boundaries

The elements of a batch MUST be processed in the following order:

  1. Lookup entries – see the working set of a batch.
  2. Namespace declarations, in order.
  3. Statements, in order.

The row_count field (1) is the number of statements (rows) in the batch. It MUST NOT be greater than 227 − 1, which is the largest number of cells the sequence layout of a column can address. The consumer MUST throw an error otherwise.

Each column stores the RDF terms of one position of the statements (subject, predicate, object, or graph name), with one cell per statement, in the order of the statements. To read a statement, take the cells at the same position in each column: the first statement of the batch is made up of the first cell of the subjects column, the first cell of the predicates column, and the first cell of the objects column (and the first cell of the graphs column, in a QUADS stream). The second statement is made up of the second cells, and so on. A column field that is not set is treated in the same way as an empty column, in which all cells are unbound. The following rules apply to the columns:

  • subjects (6) – MUST contain only IRIs and blank nodes.
  • predicates (7) – MUST contain only IRIs.
  • objects (8) – may contain IRIs, blank nodes, literals, and triple terms.
  • graphs (9) – MUST NOT be set in a stream with physical type TRIPLES. In a stream with physical type QUADS, it MUST contain only IRIs and blank nodes. An unbound cell means that the statement is in the default graph. If the field is not set, all statements of the batch are in the default graph.
  • The subjects, predicates, and objects columns MUST NOT have unbound cells. The consumer MUST throw an error if any of them has an unbound cell in the first row_count cells.
  • The consumer SHOULD throw an error if a column contains a type of RDF term that is not allowed in it.

Note

These rules mean that Jelly-RDF 1.2 cannot represent generalized RDF (e.g., literals as subjects).

Note

Most columns are cheap to encode. A batch of statements about one subject has a subjects column with one value and one repeat run. A batch of quads in one named graph has a graphs column with one value and one repeat run. A batch of quads in the default graph does not need the graphs column at all.

Example (click to expand)

Consider a stream with physical type QUADS and a batch with these three statements, in N-Quads notation with the prefix ex: used for brevity:

ex:alice ex:knows ex:bob .
ex:alice ex:name "Alice" ex:g1 .
ex:bob ex:name "Bob" ex:g1 .

The batch has row_count: 3, and its columns contain the following cells (_ marks an unbound cell):

Statement subjects predicates objects graphs 1 ex:alice ex:knows ex:bob _ (default graph) 2 ex:alice ex:name "Alice" ex:g1 3 ex:bob ex:name "Bob" ex:g1

Each of the four columns is then encoded as an RdfColumn, as described in columns. The subjects column has the run values ex:alice and ex:bob, with ex:alice taking up two cells. The objects column mixes IRIs and literals, so it needs the kinds field. See the full example for a complete encoding of a similar batch.

docs.title: Message boundaries
docs.text:
In a stream of RDF Messages (stream type RDF_STREAM_TYPE_MESSAGES), the statements of the stream are split into messages. The frame boundaries do not mark where a message ends. Instead, the ends of the messages are written explicitly, in the message_lengths field (15) of the column batches. In a stream with stream type RDF_STREAM_TYPE_FLAT, this field MUST be empty.

At any point of the stream, the current message is made up of the statements that were not yet assigned to any message. It may include statements from earlier frames. Each value of message_lengths, in order, adds that many more statements of the batch to the current message, and then ends the current message. In particular:

  • A value of 0 ends the current message without adding statements to it. If the current message has no statements, this is an empty message.
  • The sum of the values MUST NOT be greater than row_count. The consumer MUST throw an error otherwise.
  • The statements of the batch after the last boundary start the next message, which continues in the following frames.

At the end of the stream, if the current message has any statements, it ends there. If it has none, no message is added. The same applies when the stream options are restated.

Example (click to expand)

Assume that the previous frame ended with one statement, s0, that was not assigned to any message. The current batch has row_count: 5, with statements s1 to s5, and:

message_lengths: [2, 0, 1]
  • 2 – the current message (s0) gets s1 and s2, and ends. The message is s0, s1, s2.
  • 0 – the next message ends immediately. It is an empty message.
  • 1 – the next message gets s3, and ends. The message is s3.

s4 and s5 start the next message, which continues in the following frames.

Note

A producer that writes one message per frame simply sets message_lengths: [row_count] in every frame. A producer with small messages can put many of them in one frame.

docs.title: Columns
docs.text:
Columns are a general mechanism for storing sequences of RDF terms. They are used by Jelly-RDF and by Jelly-SPARQL.

A column stores the cells of one statement position (in Jelly-RDF) or one variable (in Jelly-SPARQL) across all row_count rows of a batch, in row order. A cell is either a bound RDF term or unbound. Each format defines what an unbound cell means, and where it is allowed – for Jelly-RDF, see column batches.

A column is stored as an RdfColumn message. Every column contains:

  • The run values of the column – RDF terms, with each run of consecutive equal values stored exactly once. Unbound cells are not stored. The run values are split by the type of RDF term into separate lists: IRIs, literals, blank nodes, and triple terms. The kinds field indicates which list stores each run value, see term types.
  • The layouts list – a description of where the sequence of cells deviates from "each run value occupies exactly one cell", see sequence layout.

The RdfColumn message has the following fields:

Field Contents Described in kinds (1) the term type of each run value Term types layouts (2) the sequence layout Sequence layout name_ids (3) name identifiers of the IRIs IRIs in columns prefix_ids (4) prefix identifiers of the IRIs IRIs in columns lex_values (5) lexical forms of the literals Literals in columns literal_kinds (6) literal kinds of the literals Literals in columns langtags (7) language tags of the literals Literals in columns langtag_directions (8) base directions of the language tags Literals in columns bnodes (9) blank node labels Blank nodes in columns triple_terms (10) triple terms Triple terms in columns

Each list contains the values of its type in row order, and is empty if the column has no values of that type.

A column whose cells are all unbound is encoded as an empty message. A column MUST NOT decode to more than row_count cells. If it decodes to fewer, the remaining cells at the end of the column are unbound.

docs.title: Term types
docs.text:
The kinds field packs one term type per run value into 2 bits, four run values per byte, starting from the least significant bits of the first byte:

Term type Meaning 0 The next IRI (name_ids and prefix_ids). 1 The next literal (lex_values and literal_kinds). 2 The next blank node (bnodes). 3 The next triple term (triple_terms).

The number of run values m of a column is the total number of values in its lists: len(name_ids) + len(lex_values) + len(bnodes) + len(triple_terms). The run values of the column are obtained by going through the term types in order, and taking the next value from the list of that type. Then the layouts of the column are applied to these run values.

If all run values of a column are of one type, kinds SHOULD be empty. A consumer then reads the run values from the one list that has values, in order.

The consumer MUST throw an error if any of the following is true:

  • kinds is empty, and more than one of the lists has values.
  • kinds is not empty, and does not have exactly ⌈m / 4⌉ bytes.
  • The unused bits of the last byte of kinds are not 0.
  • kinds refers to more values of a type than the list of that type has.

Note

Many columns contain terms of a single type, so they do not need the kinds field. A column with mixed types costs 2 bits per run value. The values of each type are still in flat lists: the IRIs of any column are two lists of integers, and its literals are a list of strings.

Example (click to expand)

A column containing, in five consecutive rows:

https://a.org/x
_:b1
"hello"
"hello"
https://a.org/y

Assume the prefix lookup contains https://a.org/ at id 1, and the name lookup has x at 1 and y at 2. The run values are x, _:b1, "hello", y, with the term types 0, 2, 1, 0, and "hello" occupies two cells.

RdfColumn {
    kinds: "\x18"
    # 0b00_01_10_00: IRI, blank node, literal, IRI (least significant bits first)
    layouts: [64]
    # skip = 2, repeat run of 2 cells
    name_ids: [0, 0]
    prefix_ids: [1]
    lex_values: ["hello"]
    bnodes: ["b1"]
}

docs.title: Sequence layout
docs.text:
The layouts field of every column is a flat list of exceptions to the rule "each run value occupies exactly one cell". When every cell of a column is bound and no value repeats in consecutive rows, layouts is empty.

Each exception is one varint token, optionally followed by one extension varint:

token = (skip << 5) | (kind << 4) | len_code
  • skip – bits 5 and up. The number of run values that occupy exactly one cell each since the previous exception, or since the start of the column.
  • kind – bit 4. 0 = repeat run, 1 = unbound run.
  • len_code – bits 0–3. If its value is 0–14, the run length code len is equal to it. If its value is 15, then len is 15 plus the value of the next varint in the layouts list (the extension varint).

The run lengths are interpreted as follows:

  • Repeat run – the run value at the current position occupies len + 2 cells.
  • Unbound run – there are len + 1 consecutive unbound cells.

An unbound run is before the run value at the current position, or after the last run value once all run values have been consumed. This makes the order of an unbound run and a repeat run at the same position unambiguous.

Decoding a column proceeds as follows, where m is the number of run values and n is row_count:

i = 0      # index into the run values
pos = 0    # index into the cells

for each exception (skip, kind, len) in layouts:
    emit run values i .. i+skip, one cell each;  i += skip;  pos += skip
    if kind == 0:   # repeat run
        emit run value i into (len + 2) cells;  i += 1;  pos += len + 2
    else:           # unbound run
        emit (len + 1) unbound cells;  pos += len + 1

emit run values i .. m, one cell each      # implicit tail
emit unbound cells until pos == n          # padding

A batch is corrupt, and the consumer MUST throw an error, if any of the following is true for any of its columns:

  • i + skip > m – a skip runs past the last run value.
  • A repeat run starts when i == m – the run points past the last run value.
  • len_code is 15 and the token is not followed by an extension varint.
  • The column decodes to more than row_count cells.

Producers SHOULD merge adjacent runs. In particular, a producer SHOULD NOT emit two unbound runs separated by skip == 0. Producers SHOULD omit trailing unbound runs and rely on the padding rule instead (see: Columns).

Consumers MUST decode a column in which runs were not merged (e.g., equal values in consecutive cells stored as separate run values) as described above, with each run value in its own cells.

Note

A token stays a single byte as long as skip <= 3. Repeat runs of up to 16 cells and unbound runs of up to 15 cells fit in the token without an extension varint.

The skip field occupies the upper 27 bits of the token, which is where the maximum row count of 227 − 1 comes from.

Example (click to expand)

Consider a column of 8 cells with the following contents (_ marks an unbound cell):

A  B  B  B  _  _  C  C

The run values are A, B, C – three values for eight cells. The layout is:

  • skip = 1 (the single A), kind = 0 (repeat run), len = 1 (because B occupies 1 + 2 = 3 cells) → token = (1 << 5) | (0 << 4) | 1 = 33.
  • skip = 0, kind = 1 (unbound run), len = 1 (because there are 1 + 1 = 2 unbound cells) → token = (0 << 5) | (1 << 4) | 1 = 17.
  • skip = 0, kind = 0 (repeat run), len = 0 (because C occupies 0 + 2 = 2 cells) → token = 0.

So layouts = [33, 17, 0].

Now consider a column of 42 cells: A, then B repeated 40 times, then C. The repeat run of B needs len = 40 − 2 = 38, which does not fit in len_code. So len_code = 15, and the extension varint is 38 − 15 = 23:

  • skip = 1 (the single A), kind = 0 (repeat run), len_code = 15 → token = (1 << 5) | (0 << 4) | 15 = 47, followed by the extension varint 23.

The C at the end is covered by the implicit tail, so layouts = [47, 23].

docs.title: IRIs in columns
docs.text:
The IRIs of a column are stored in two fields of RdfColumn:

  • name_ids (3) – the name identifiers of the IRIs, in row order. The length of this list is the number of IRIs among the run values.
  • prefix_ids (4) – the prefix identifiers of the IRIs, in row order.

The IRIs are reconstructed as described in IRIs.

The IRIs of a column are one IRI sequence, which starts at the start of the column, in every batch. The name_ids list follows the name_id inference rule: a value of 0 means "previous name_id + 1", and in the first IRI of the column it means name_id = 1.

The prefix_ids list MUST have one of three lengths:

Length Meaning 0 Every IRI has prefix_id = 0, that is, no prefix. This is the case when the prefix lookup is disabled. 1 Every IRI uses the prefix given by the single entry. This is the case for a column of IRIs sharing one namespace. len(name_ids) One entry per IRI.

In the third form, the prefix_id inference rule applies along the list: a value of 0 means "the same prefix as the previous IRI in this column", and in the first IRI of the column it means no prefix.

The consumer MUST throw an error if the length of prefix_ids is none of the three allowed values.

Example (click to expand)

A column containing four IRIs, in four consecutive rows:

https://a.org/x1
https://a.org/x2
https://a.org/x1
https://b.org/z

Assume the prefix lookup contains https://a.org/ at id 1 and https://b.org/ at id 2, and the name lookup contains x1 at 1, x2 at 2, and z at 3.

RdfColumn {
    name_ids: [0, 0, 1, 3]
    # 0 -> 0 + 1 = 1 (x1)
    # 0 -> 1 + 1 = 2 (x2)
    # 1 -> 1      (x1)
    # 3 -> 3      (z)
    prefix_ids: [1, 0, 0, 2]
    # 0 means "same prefix as the previous IRI"
    # kinds is empty: every value is an IRI
    # layouts is empty: every cell is bound, no two consecutive cells are equal
}

The same column in a batch where every IRI is in the https://a.org/ namespace would have prefix_ids: [1] instead – one entry for the whole column.

docs.title: Literals in columns
docs.text:
The literals of a column are stored in four fields of RdfColumn:

  • lex_values (5) – the lexical forms of the literals, in row order. The length of this list is the number of literals among the run values.
  • literal_kinds (6) – the literal kinds of the literals, in row order, see below.
  • langtags (7) – the language tags that the literal kinds refer to, as UTF-8 strings.
  • langtag_directions (8) – the base directions of the language tags, parallel to langtags, as RdfBaseDirection values.

Each literal is a lexical form plus a literal kind, which indicates what type of literal it is. A literal kind is an unsigned integer v:

Literal kind v Meaning 0 A simple literal, that is, a literal with the datatype http://www.w3.org/2001/XMLSchema#string. odd v A literal with the datatype of the datatype lookup entry with identifier (v + 1) / 2. even v > 0 A language-tagged string with the language tag langtags[v / 2 − 1] (a 0-based index), and the base direction langtag_directions[v / 2 − 1].

The literal_kinds list MUST have one of three lengths:

Length Meaning 0 Every literal is a simple literal. 1 Every literal has the literal kind given by the single entry. This is the case for a column of values that share one datatype, or one language tag and base direction. len(lex_values) One entry per literal.

The consumer MUST throw an error if the length of literal_kinds is none of the three allowed values, or if a literal kind refers to an index past the end of langtags.

The following rules apply to the language tags:

  • Each entry of langtags SHOULD be a valid BCP 47 language tag.
  • Producers SHOULD list the language tags in the order in which the literals first use them, and SHOULD NOT list a language tag that is not used by any literal.
  • The same language tag MAY appear in langtags more than once, with different base directions. Producers SHOULD NOT list the same pair of language tag and base direction twice.
  • langtag_directions MUST be empty, or have exactly as many entries as langtags. An empty list means that no language tag of the column has a base direction. The consumer MUST throw an error if the list has any other length.
  • Consumers are not required to check the entries of langtag_directions that are not used by any literal.
  • Producers SHOULD leave langtag_directions empty in a stream that declares RDF_VERSION_1_1, because such a stream has no base directions.

A literal kind that refers to a datatype MUST NOT refer to an entry containing http://www.w3.org/1999/02/22-rdf-syntax-ns#langString or http://www.w3.org/1999/02/22-rdf-syntax-ns#dirLangString, because a literal with that datatype and no language tag is not a valid RDF term. Language-tagged strings always use a language tag from langtags. The consumer SHOULD throw an error otherwise.

A simple literal does not need an xsd:string entry in the datatype lookup: the producer can use the literal kind 0 instead. A literal kind referring to an xsd:string entry is also legal and produces the same result.

Note

This design allows for efficiently storing columns in which every value has the same literal kind – think of a column of xsd:integer values, or a column of language strings in one language.

Example (click to expand)

Consider a column containing, in four consecutive rows:

"cat"@en
"42"^^xsd:integer
"chat"@fr
"dog"@en

Assume the datatype lookup contains xsd:integer at id 1.

RdfColumn {
    lex_values: ["cat", "42", "chat", "dog"]
    literal_kinds: [2, 1, 4, 2]
    # 2 -> langtags[0] (en)
    # 1 -> datatype 1 (xsd:integer)
    # 4 -> langtags[1] (fr)
    langtags: ["en", "fr"]
    # langtag_directions is empty: no base directions
    # kinds is empty: every value is a literal
}

A column of the same four rows, but with every value tagged @en, would have literal_kinds: [2] and langtags: ["en"] instead.

docs.title: Blank nodes in columns
docs.text: The blank nodes of a column are stored in the bnodes field (9) of RdfColumn: the blank node labels, in row order, as plain UTF-8 strings.

docs.title: Triple terms in columns
docs.text:
The triple terms of a column are stored in the triple_terms field (10) of RdfColumn, as RdfTripleTerm messages, in row order. Triple terms cannot occur in a stream that declares RDF_VERSION_1_1 or RDF_VERSION_1_2_BASIC. If triple_terms is not empty in such a stream, the consumer MAY throw an error (see RDF version).

The IRIs of all the triple terms of one column are one IRI sequence, which starts at the start of the column, in every batch. It advances through the triple terms in order, and through the IRIs of each triple term in the order subject, predicate, object, recursively into nested triple terms. This sequence is separate from the sequence of the other IRIs of the column (name_ids and prefix_ids). See triple terms for how a triple term and its nested triple terms are encoded, and IRIs for the inference rules of an IRI sequence.

docs.title: IRIs
docs.text:
An IRI is encoded as two identifiers: a prefix identifier, referring to an entry in the prefix lookup, and a name identifier, referring to an entry in the name lookup. In columns, the identifiers are stored in lists. In triple terms and namespace declarations, they are stored in an RdfIri message, which has two fields:

  • prefix_id (1) – 1-based identifier of the prefix of the IRI, corresponding to an entry in the prefix lookup.
  • name_id (2) – 1-based identifier of the name (suffix) of the IRI, corresponding to an entry in the name lookup.

Both identifiers may be written as 0, in which case their value is inferred from the previous IRI. The inference works along an IRI sequence: a series of IRIs, processed in a fixed order. Each place where IRIs are stored defines its own IRI sequences:

  • The IRIs of a column (name_ids and prefix_ids) – one sequence per column, per batch. See IRIs in columns.
  • The IRIs in the triple terms of a column – one sequence per column, per batch. See triple terms in columns.
  • The IRIs of the namespace declarations – one sequence per batch. See namespace declarations.

Within an IRI sequence, the following rules apply:

  • A name_id of 0 MUST be interpreted as previous_name_id + 1, that is, the name identifier of the previous IRI in the sequence incremented by one. In the first IRI of the sequence, it MUST be interpreted as 1. Multiple 0 values in a row may occur, in which case the name identifier MUST be interpreted as incrementing by one for each 0 value.
  • A prefix_id of 0 MUST be interpreted as the same prefix identifier as in the previous IRI of the sequence. In the first IRI of the sequence, it MUST be interpreted as no prefix (an empty, zero-length string). This is for example used when the prefix lookup table is disabled.

The IRI is then constructed by first resolving the prefix and the name using the prefix and name lookup tables, and then concatenating the prefix and the name. The IRI SHOULD be a valid IRI, as defined in RFC 3987.

Difference from Jelly-RDF 1.1

In Jelly-RDF 1.1, there is one IRI sequence for the whole stream, in the strict order of rows and terms. In Jelly-RDF 1.2, there is one sequence per column, per batch. This lets a consumer decode the columns of a batch in any order, or in parallel, given only the lookup tables.

Note

The spec does not specify how to split the IRIs into names and prefixes. You can use any strategy you want, as long as you follow the rules above. The simplest way is to split the IRI at the last occurrence of the # or / character – this is what the Java implementation uses.

These prefixes are not meant to be user-facing, they can be entirely arbitrary and DO NOT correspond to, for example, PREFIX declarations in Turtle. If you want to preserve such user-facing namespace declarations, use the namespace declarations feature instead.

Note

The behavior of the default values is designed to save space in the stream. Usually in RDF many IRIs share the same prefix, so you can save space by not repeating the prefix in the stream. At the same time the name part of the IRI is often unique, so for each name you will need a new entry in the lookup table – which is often the next entry after the one you have just created.

docs.title: Literals
docs.text:
Literals in columns are stored in lists. Literals in the object position of triple terms are stored as RdfLiteral messages, which have the following fields:

  • lex (1) – the lexical form of the literal in UTF-8. This field is OPTIONAL and defaults to an empty string.
  • literalKind oneof. At most one of the following fields MUST be set:
    • langtag (2) – UTF-8 language tag, indicating that the literal is a language-tagged string. The language tag SHOULD be a valid BCP 47 language tag.
    • datatype (3) – 1-based identifier of the datatype in the datatype lookup, indicating that the literal is a typed literal.
  • direction (4) – the base direction of a language-tagged string.

If no field in the literalKind oneof is set, then the literal MUST be interpreted as a simple literal (has datatype IRI equal to http://www.w3.org/2001/XMLSchema#string).

The following rules apply:

  • direction MUST NOT be set unless langtag is set. The consumer MUST throw an error otherwise.
  • datatype MUST NOT be 0, and MUST NOT refer to rdf:langString or rdf:dirLangString. The consumer MUST throw an error if it is 0, and SHOULD throw an error if it refers to rdf:langString or rdf:dirLangString.

Note

Using the default value of 0 for the datatype field is not allowed, in contrast to names and prefixes in RdfIri. This is because the datatype field itself is optional and the default value would be ambiguous.

docs.title: Base direction
docs.text:
In RDF 1.2, a language-tagged string may have a base direction: ltr (left-to-right) or rtl (right-to-left). Such a literal has the datatype http://www.w3.org/1999/02/22-rdf-syntax-ns#dirLangString.

A base direction is an RdfBaseDirection value: RDF_BASE_DIRECTION_UNSPECIFIED (0, the default: no base direction), RDF_BASE_DIRECTION_LTR (1), or RDF_BASE_DIRECTION_RTL (2). It is encoded in the langtag_directions field of columns, and in the direction field of RdfLiteral.

The following rules apply:

  • The consumer SHOULD throw an error if the base direction of a literal has a value that is not listed above.
  • A stream that declares RDF_VERSION_1_1 MUST NOT contain a literal with a base direction other than RDF_BASE_DIRECTION_UNSPECIFIED.

docs.title: Blank nodes
docs.text:
RDF blank nodes are represented using their labels: simple UTF-8 strings.

Blank node labels are scoped as follows:

  • In a stream with stream type RDF_STREAM_TYPE_FLAT, the scope is the whole stream, also across restated stream options.
  • In a stream with stream type RDF_STREAM_TYPE_MESSAGES, the scope is one RDF Message.

Two occurrences of the same label within one scope MUST be interpreted as referring to the same blank node. Two different labels MUST be interpreted as referring to different blank nodes. Two occurrences of the same label in different scopes MUST be interpreted as referring to different blank nodes.

Note

Many RDF libraries (e.g., Eclipse RDF4J, Apache Jena) use internal identifiers for blank nodes, which can be used as the labels in Jelly streams. You can also use a different format, for example with shorter labels to preserve space.

docs.title: Triple terms
docs.text:
An RDF 1.2 triple term is encoded as an RdfTripleTerm message. Triple terms may occur only in the objects column of a column batch (see column batches), and as objects of other triple terms. RdfTripleTerm has the following fields:

  • the subject oneof – s_iri (1), an RdfIri, or s_bnode (2), a blank node label.
  • p_iri (5) – the predicate, an RdfIri.
  • the object oneof – o_iri (9), an RdfIri; o_bnode (10), a blank node label; o_literal (11), an RdfLiteral; or o_triple_term (12), a nested RdfTripleTerm.

The following rules apply:

  • The subject, the predicate, and the object MUST all be set. The consumer MUST throw an error if any of them is missing.
  • The IRIs in the triple terms follow the rules of the IRI sequence of the triple terms of their column, see triple terms in columns.
  • Triple terms may be nested up to arbitrary depth. The consumer SHOULD throw an error if the depth of the nesting exceeds the capabilities of the implementation.

docs.title: Namespace declarations
docs.text:
